title: 17akhf7
The Feet in Ablution: Wiping or Washing?
hook: How do the two readings of Mâide 6 open the feet in ablution to wiping and to washing?
scenes.0.text: Mâide 6 lists the limbs of ablution: the face, the hands up to the elbows, a wiping of part of the head, and the feet up to the ankles. The word "your feet" has been read with two different vowelings. Both readings are known in the tradition of recitation. The Ja'fari school reads this verse as wiping the feet.
scenes.0.art.actors.0.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.1.text: In the fatha reading, the word appears to be linked to the limbs that are washed; in the kasra reading, to the neighboring word "your heads." The first reading is closer to washing, the second to wiping. It is reported that both readings are among the seven recitations. The Ja'fari school continues the kasra reading as a command to wipe the feet.
scenes.1.art.actors.0.label: 5y6q5g
Reciter
scenes.1.art.actors.1.label: 1feddiq
Grammarian
scenes.2.text: In narrations from the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, the wiping is done on top of the foot, from the tips of the toes to the ankle; the foot is not washed. Tusi's Tahdhib and Kulayni's al-Kafi are mentioned among the sources of this view. The texts could not be opened in this study. The Ja'fari school applies Mâide 6 as wiping of the feet with these narrations.
scenes.2.art.actors.0.label: lhg99z
Imam Ali
scenes.2.art.actors.1.label: nsaem3
Student
scenes.3.text: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet said, "Woe to the heels from the Fire" (Bukhari, Sahih, No. 165). The same warning comes also through Abdullah b. Amr (Muslim, Sahih). In Caliph Uthman's description of ablution, it is also stated that the feet were washed (Bukhari, Sahih; Muslim, Sahih). The Ja'fari school reads these sayings as a warning to clean the foot thoroughly and continues to apply **Mâide 6** as wiping of the feet.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: kjrlmg
Person performing ablution
scenes.3.art.actors.1.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.4.text: In Ibn Majah, when Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh relates that the Prophet washed his feet, Ibn Abbas says that people insist on washing, while he finds only wiping in the Book of God. The chain of the narration has been deemed weak, and Ibn Abbas's statement has been found munkar by al-Albani. The view of wiping is also attributed to Imam Ali, Anas, Hasan al-Basri, Ikrima, al-Sha'bi and Abu al-Aliya. For al-Tabari, a choice between wiping and washing is reported; for al-Jubba'i, the view of wiping. IslamQA addresses only the reports of Imam Ali, Ibn Abbas and Anas among these. The Ja'fari school continues the practice of wiping the feet with this early reading.
scenes.4.art.actors.0.label: 19xa2pv
Rubayyi'
scenes.4.art.actors.1.label: 1q0thws
Ibn Abbas
scenes.5.text: In Ja'fari commentary, the kasra reading is regarded as the reading most suited to the flow of the verse. Tabataba'i and Makarim Shirazi also prefer this reading. According to the explanation of the neighboring word taking the kasra, jarr al-jiwar, when there is a "and" in between, the effect of adjacency is regarded as weak in terms of language. Wiping and washing are two separate acts. If wiping included washing, washing would suffice for the head as well. The Ja'fari school applies this distinction as wiping of the feet.
scenes.5.art.actors.0.label: li7v2o
Commentator
scenes.5.art.actors.1.label: 1feddiq
Grammarian
scenes.6.text: In some schools of jurisprudence, wiping over leather socks is considered permissible even in ordinary circumstances. In Ja'fari jurisprudence, wiping is done on the bare foot; wiping over leather socks is permissible only under taqiyya or in a case of necessity. Tabataba'i, relying on some narrations, writes that Mâide 6 abrogated the Prophet's earlier wiping over leather socks.

scenes.7.text: The feet in ablution open into two practices according to the two readings. Ja'fari jurisprudence wipes the top of the foot and regards this as the reading of the verse and of the narrations of the Ahl al-Bayt. The majority of the Sunni schools wash the feet. Both bring evidence from the verse and the narrations. The difference lies in the reading, the evaluation of narrations and the choice of language.

disputes.0.title: 1h5zsns
"Your feet": fatha or kasra?
disputes.0.shia: In Mâide 6, "your feet" is read with both vowelings. In the Ja'fari reading, the kasra is a command to wipe the feet; the fatha reading can also be taken to wiping by linking it to the place of the head.
disputes.0.sunni: In Mâide 6, "your feet" is read with both vowelings. In the Sunni reading, the fatha points to washing; the kasra is interpreted as washing through adjacency, the hadiths or light washing.
disputes.1.title: 1qeerqi
The grammatical interpretation of jarr al-jiwar
disputes.1.shia: The kasra reading is the subject of two grammatical explanations. In the Ja'fari grammatical choice, when a "and" intervenes, the kasra of adjacency is weak.
disputes.1.sunni: The kasra reading is the subject of two grammatical explanations. In the Sunni explanation, the kasra agrees with the neighboring "your heads"; the meaning is washing.
disputes.2.title: gnpmxe
"Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution
disputes.2.shia: The warning "Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution also appear in Sunni books. The Ja'fari reading regards these hadiths as a warning to clean the foot well; the Ahl al-Bayt narrations report wiping.
disputes.2.sunni: The warning "Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution also appear in Sunni books. In this account, the hadiths show that the Prophet washed his feet, and the verse is read in line with this practice.
disputes.3.title: 24v2t2
Wiping over leather socks
disputes.3.shia: Wiping over leather socks is mentioned in both jurisprudences. In Ja'fari practice, wiping is done on the bare foot; the verse is accepted as having abrogated the earlier wiping over leather socks.
disputes.3.sunni: Wiping over leather socks is mentioned in both jurisprudences. In the Sunni schools, this wiping is regarded as a permissible sunna even in ordinary circumstances.
questions.0: Since Mâide 6 has two recitations, how are the flow of the verse and the Prophet's practice read together to link one reading to the other?
questions.1: The chain of the saying "I find wiping in the Book of God," attributed to Ibn Abbas, has been found weak. What does a weak saying still tell us about the history of the debate?
questions.2: In the explanation of jarr al-jiwar, how does the particle "and" in between affect the view that the kasra comes from adjacency?
questions.3: The hadith "Woe to the heels from the Fire" emphasizes which part of the foot must not be neglected? What does the context of the narration tell you?
summary: The two recitations of Mâide 6 open the door to wiping and washing the feet. Ja'fari jurisprudence wipes the top of the foot. The majority of the Sunni schools regard washing as obligatory. Some Sunni reports also relate the view of wiping.
key: Washing the feet or wiping them?
notes.1: The word «your feet» is read with two recitations: fatha (washing) and kasra (wiping).
notes.2: The Sunni schools wash the feet.
notes.3: Ja'fari jurisprudence, following the wiping reading of the verse, wipes over the feet.
notes.4: Practice also differs on wiping over leather socks; both schools base ablution on the Qur'an.
